summary: Describes using the Predictor data compression algorithm to compress PPP packets. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A method that guesses what comes next and only sends the surprises, so less data has to travel.

what is the guess table in predictor
what are predictor type 1 and type 2 encapsulation
subtitle: A fast, license-free compression algorithm for PPP links.

tldr.problem: PPP compression algorithms require licenses or patent clearances. A fast, royalty-free compression method would be valuable, even if it sacrifices some compression ratio.
tldr.mechanism: Predictor works by maintaining a guess table indexed by a rolling hash of previous characters. For each byte, it either outputs the byte or marks it as correctly guessed, depending on whether the guess table prediction was right. A flag byte precedes every 8 bytes of output to indicate which were guessed.
tldr.outcome: Predictor provides license-free compression available for any implementation. It trades smaller compression ratios for higher speed and freedom from licensing restrictions.

today: RFC 1978 is Informational. Predictor compression became widely used in dial-up modem implementations because of its license-free nature and reasonable speed, despite modest compression ratios. Modern systems typically use more advanced algorithms, but Predictor remains a simple, patent-unencumbered choice for systems where compression licensing is not feasible.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Predictor data compression algorithm offers high-speed compression available without license fees. Unlike proprietary compression algorithms, Predictor can be freely implemented in any PPP system without royalty concerns, though the trade-off is that it achieves a lower compression ratio than algorithms like LZ77 variants.

The RFC includes reference C code for both compression and decompression. Although the algorithm takes care to avoid known patent infringements, implementers are cautioned that no assurance of patent-freedom can be given.
sections.plainLanguage: Predictor is a squishing method anyone can use for free. It is fast but does not make things as small as fancy squishing does.

sections.title: How Predictor Works
sections.content:
Predictor maintains a table of 65,536 entries indexed by a rolling hash computed from the previous characters. To compress, for each byte of input, the algorithm checks if the value in the guess table at the hash index matches the input byte. If it matches, a bit in the flag byte is set to indicate a correct guess. If it does not match, the algorithm outputs the byte and updates the table entry to remember it. A flag byte precedes every 8 bytes of reconstructed data.

Decompression reverses this process: for each flag byte indicating 8 predictions, the decompressor either reconstructs the byte from the guess table or reads it from the compressed stream, updating the table each time. The flag byte tells it which to do for each position.

The hash function is simple: Hash = (Hash << 4) ^ (byte). This rolling hash provides a quick index into the guess table based on recent history.
sections.plainLanguage: Predictor keeps a big table of guesses. For each byte, it asks the table: did you guess this right? If yes, skip the byte. If no, send it and update your guess.

sections.title: Encapsulation Formats
sections.content:
Predictor defines two encapsulation types. Type 1 is for packet-by-packet compression: each packet contains the PPP protocol identifier (always 0xFD), a 1-bit compressed flag followed by 15 bits of the uncompressed data length in octets, the compressed data, and a CRC-16 checksum of the two-octet length field.

Type 2 is for streaming compression: the packet contains the protocol identifier, followed by multiple frames, each with its own length field, compressed data, and CRC-16. Type 2 allows the data stream to be broken at any convenient place for encapsulation. The RFC notes that Type 2 is almost essential to use with a reliable link protocol like LAPB to ensure correct delivery.

In both types, the compressed data includes the Protocol Identifier and Information fields of the original PPP packet, but not the Address, Control, FCS, or Flag fields. If the decompressor detects a CRC-16 mismatch, it indicates desynchronization, requiring a new CCP configure-request to reset the compression tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Type 1 wraps each squished packet with its length and checksum. Type 2 packs multiple squished frames into one packet. If a checksum fails, both sides clear their guesses and start over.

sections.title: Compression and Decompression Operation
sections.content:
Before Predictor packets can be communicated, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the Compression Control Protocol must reach the Opened state. Exactly one Predictor datagram is encapsulated in the PPP Information field with protocol type 0xFD.

The compressor processes input in 8-byte blocks, maintaining both the hash state and the 65,536-byte guess table. The decompressor mirrors this operation, reconstructing the original data byte by byte and updating its guess table in sync with the compressor.

Predictor packets must not contain PPP Link Control Protocol frames. If a frame is lost and the guess tables become desynchronized, the CRC-16 check will fail, signaling the need to reset both tables via the CCP negotiation mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides keep identical guess tables and update them the same way. If data is lost, the mismatched checksum tells them to clear the tables and start fresh.

sections.title: Configuration and Deployment
sections.content:
Predictor has no configuration options for type 1 or type 2. The RFC provides reference C code that can be used directly in implementations. A simple 8 KB compression buffer is sufficient for the guess table.

The RFC explicitly states that Predictor uses the code at implementers' own risk, with no assurance of patent freedom. The algorithm was originally implemented by Timo Raita. Despite these caveats, Predictor was widely adopted in dial-up modem compression due to its speed and freedom from licensing restrictions, making it a practical choice for systems where compression licenses were costly.
sections.plainLanguage: No setup needed beyond saying you want to use Predictor. The guessing method is fixed. The code is public and free to use.
